records.quote: That has made piracy a thing of the past.
records.paraphrase: The captain claims wireless technology has ended piracy.

records.quote: It was packed--not with Bibles--but with nitroglycerin.
records.paraphrase: The chests believed to hold Bibles are revealed to contain nitroglycerin.

records.quote: If these men were what they said they were, the two big chests below, which common report had it were filled with Bibles, would prove their case. I suggested, therefore, that we examine these two chests.
records.paraphrase: Jim proposes testing his suspicion by inspecting the chests to see whether they contain Bibles as claimed.

records.quote: Literally before our eyes they vanished in a great sheet of flame. I had a momentary glimpse of the yacht apparently splitting in two, and then the roar of a gigantic explosion nearly deafened me.
records.paraphrase: The pirates' yacht is destroyed in a huge explosion.

records.quote: Has it occurred to you,\u201d said Jim quietly, \u201cthat two very useful pieces of information have been included in those two fool messages? First, our exact position at a given time, and our course and our speed.
records.paraphrase: Jim deduces that the seemingly foolish wireless messages actually transmitted the ship's position, course, and speed.

criteria.rationale: References to Marconi wireless and nitroglycerin are ordinary period technology and mundane chemistry, not a materially represented scientific fact, theory, discovery, or speculative science.

Wireless telegraphy is used as a tool of the pirates' scheme (transmitting position/course/speed), and the nitroglycerin boxes with clockwork timing mechanisms are engineered devices central to the plot and its resolution.
The story is set in a contemporary (early twentieth-century) period; there is no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement.

Jim extrapolates the pirates' plan from the wireless clues and swaps the cargo, but this is plot reasoning from a criminal scheme rather than consequences developed from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise; materiality of the extrapolation as a genuine SF premise is uncertain.

Jim forms a hypothesis that the parsons are not genuine, infers meaning from the wireless messages, and proposes a concrete test (examining the chests) to confirm or refute it, materially driving the action.
The setting is the Indian Ocean aboard ordinary ships; there are no other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them.

A large explosion destroys the yacht and kills all aboard, and the averted plan would have sunk the Andaman with all hands; it is a violent destructive event but confined in scale to a single vessel rather than a clearly large-scale disaster.

candidates.description: Shipboard wireless (Marconi) telegraphy, portrayed by the captain as a technology that has 'made piracy a thing of the past' by enabling ships to summon help and report positions.

novelty.rationale: Wireless telegraphy was a real, contemporaneous technology (explicitly credited to Marconi) at the story's period. It does not represent a totalizing difference from the author's empirical norm; it is part of the mundane early-twentieth-century world. The claim that it ended piracy is presented as ordinary opinion, not a world-altering imaginary innovation.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The wireless is treated coherently and systematically: it transmits position, course, and speed, which Jim rationally deduces the pirates exploited. Its operation is consistent and nonsupernatural.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The wireless is an important plot device (the pirates use it to relay the ship's position; wrecking it is part of the holdup), but the overriding narrative logic is the pirate deception and the swapped-cargo counterplot rather than the wireless itself. It functions as an enabling instrument, not the governing difference.

estrangement.rationale: The captain's confidence that wireless has ended piracy sets up the reader-facing irony that a modern pirate gang instead weaponizes that same technology.

candidates.description: A gang disguised as missionaries who, using wireless-relayed position data, nitroglycerin timed with clockwork mechanisms hidden in 'Bible' chests, and an armed yacht, execute a modern high-seas piracy of a specie shipment.

novelty.rationale: The disguised-pirate scheme uses only period-plausible means (revolvers, a gun-mounted yacht, nitroglycerin, clockwork timers). It is a criminal intrigue within the ordinary empirical world, not a totalizing or world-altering difference from the author's reality. This is an adventure/mystery premise, not a Suvinian novum.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The plot is rationally and systematically explained: Jim deduces the coded wireless messages, the chests are inspected empirically, the clockwork detonator is described mechanically, and the counterplot of swapping cargoes follows logically and nonsupernaturally.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The disguised-missionary piracy scheme drives the entire narrative from suspicion through detection, counterplot, and the yacht's destruction. It governs the story's logic.

estrangement.rationale: The reveal that the 'Bible' chests hold nitroglycerin rather than scripture is a striking reader-facing contrast, but it remains an intrigue twist within the mundane world rather than a world-altering novum.
